newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy coalition wins latest budget confidence vote.
newsitem.headline: Italy coalition wins latest budget confidence vote.

text.p: Italy's centre-left government won another confidence vote in the Senate on its 1997 budget on Wednesday.
It was the fourth confidence test for Prime Minister Romano Prodi this week in the upper house, where a welter of amendments had put Thursday's deadline for approval at risk.
The government won the vote with a count of 165 votes for, six against and one abstention. The latest vote concerned the part of the budget which sets spending limits.
Media mogul Silvio Berlusconi's centre-right Freedom Alliance boycotted the ballot to protest against the austerity package.
The Senate has now approved the main bulk of the budget and the whole package might be fully ratified by the upper house by the end of Wednesday.
The bill will then pass for a further reading to the Chamber of Deputies (lower house). Under Italian law, the budget must be approved by both houses by December 31.

The government's decision to call a vote tempered enthusiasm that relations between government and opposition could be heading for a thaw following cross-party unity in the lower house on Tuesday night in voting on Italy's broadcasting system.

Prodi's Olive Tree coalition, in office since May, and Berlusconi's Freedom Alliance bloc voted the same way for the first time in parliament when the Chamber of Deputies approved stop-gap broadcasting measures.
But the budget, centrepiece of Italy's annual legislative diet, has always proved a bitter battleground between the government and the opposition.
Prodi won three confidence votes on the budget held in swift succession on Monday.
The unusually tough budget aims to slash 62.5 trillion lire ($41 billion) from the 1997 deficit with much of the emphasis on revenue-raising measures including an unpopular "Euro-tax" levy.
The budget is designed to try to squeeze Italy into Europe's planned single currency from the start.

Tuesday's broadcasting vote extends Berlusconi's right to operate three television networks by four months until the end of next May pending fuller legislation, effectively suspending measures that could have put one of his channels off air.

Politicians on both sides of the divide gave a cautious welcome to the cooperative basis of the bill, with some saying the example could bode well for action on vital constitutional reform that has until now hit deadlock.

The broadcasting vote was also the first time that the Communist Refoundation party, whose external support ensures Prodi's majority in the Chamber, had broken ranks with the government. It has branded the measures a gift to Berlusconi.

The opposition, and some forces in the Olive Tree coalition, have voiced deep unease at Prodi's reliance on Communist Refoundation, saying it makes his government hostage to a hardline minority party.
